personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Dumbledore is calm, measured, and quietly authoritative. He speaks with deliberate clarity, uses gentle irony, and deploys warmth strategically — twinkling eyes, small smiles, understated humor ('a delicious-looking custard tart I want to sample'). He is perceptive rather than reactive: when Harry lies about the car, Dumbledore 'asked no questions,' letting the omission stand. He is firm under pressure (opposing Fudge and Malfoy with controlled fire: 'his blue eyes were full of a fire Harry had never seen before'), but rarely raises his voice. His restraint is itself expressive — Harry 'hated the disappointment in his voice' more than any shout. He also displays philosophical depth in private moments (the 'it is our choices' speech). His humor is dry and unexpected ('Impaled upon your own sword, Gilderoy!'), never broad. He is simultaneously reassuring and unsettling — Harry always feels X-rayed by him.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core voice well. Dumbledore's calm interruption of Snape in the office scene ('They are not') is direct and authoritative. His custard tart line is retained verbatim. The Colin Creevey scene ('It means our students are in great danger, Minerva') adds urgency but retains dignity. His gentle handling of Ginny ('Wiser wizards than you have been hoodwinked') and the twinkling reward scene for Harry and Ron are largely faithful. The 'choices, not abilities' speech is compressed but its tone — calm, warm, philosophically weighty — is preserved. The confrontation with Lucius Malfoy in Hagrid's hut is steely and controlled, consistent with the book's 'fire in his blue eyes' beat. The film does not make him comic, passive, or heroic in ways the books don't support.
personality_voice.difference: Minor compressions: the film removes Dumbledore's silent observation of Harry's lie about the car (book scene 17), which shows his penetrating patience. The film also slightly reduces the layered tension of the post-Chamber private conversation — in the book, Dumbledore waits, considers, and draws Harry out more slowly. The film's Dumbledore is marginally more declarative and slightly less withholding, but not substantially different in register. The 'not the question' line (book: 'The question is not who... the question is how') is cut and replaced with a simpler declaration about danger, losing a small but characteristic piece of his elliptical reasoning.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The loss of the 'car lie' scene and the elliptical 'not who but how' line are small compressions that remove texture but not defining traits. The dominant personality — calm authority, dry wit, warm restraint, philosophical weight — is preserved across multiple scenes. A minor deduction for the slight flattening of his oblique, withholding quality.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: Dumbledore serves several interlocking functions in CoS: (1) institutional anchor — his presence or absence sets the threat level for the school; (2) moral and judicial authority — he alone sees through Snape's pressure and protects Harry, he defends Hagrid against Fudge and Malfoy, he dispenses punishment and reward; (3) epistemic guide — he interprets events (the Chamber being open again, the significance of Riddle's diary, the Parseltongue explanation, the 'choices' lesson); (4) indirect protector — his departure creates the vacuum of danger; his parting words ('help will always be given at Hogwarts to those who ask for it') function as a plot mechanism that calls Fawkes. He initiates several key moments: he is the one who examines Mrs. Norris, diagnoses Petrification, and makes the chamber-open declaration. He actively outwits Malfoy at the end with the diary confrontation, cornering him without proof ('one only hopes no more of Lord Voldemort's old school things find their way into innocent hands').
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves most of these functions. Dumbledore diagnoses Petrification, defends Harry ('Innocent until proven guilty'), defends Hagrid, delivers the 'choices' speech, and confronts Malfoy with the same controlled threat. The 'help will always be given' line is retained with the added beat of Dumbledore's eyes drifting unmistakably to Harry — arguably a slight improvement in clarity of agency. The reward scene and Hagrid's release are intact.
narrative_role_agency.difference: One meaningful agency loss: in the books, the post-Chamber scene includes Dumbledore actively questioning Harry ('I must ask you, Harry, whether there is anything you'd like to tell me — anything at all'), which Harry deflects. This exchange reveals Dumbledore's investigative awareness and the limits of his omniscience. In the film, this beat is retained but is shorter and less probing. More significantly, in the book Dumbledore's confrontation with Malfoy includes a more elaborated rhetorical trap — he walks Malfoy through the consequences of the diary's use, imagining what would have happened to the Weasley family, systematically dismantling Malfoy's deniability. The film compresses this to a chill warning and a push of the diary, losing the step-by-step intellectual demolition that is a key expression of Dumbledore's agency. This is a noticeable but not major compression.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: The Malfoy confrontation compression reduces one of Dumbledore's most active and precise moments of agency — he is not just confronting Malfoy, he is performing a logical prosecution. This is partially transferred to implication rather than explicit dialogue. Minor deduction for this compression; the role and its other functions are substantially intact.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Dumbledore's motivations in CoS are primarily protective and institutional: he wants to keep the school safe, protect the vulnerable (Muggle-borns, Harry, Hagrid), and maintain justice against political pressure. He is also guided by a long-term intelligence — he has known Riddle, watched him, and suspects deeper currents. There is no explicit internal conflict dramatized in the CoS book; his motivations are coherent and purposeful. His willingness to be suspended ('if the governors want my removal, I shall of course step aside') is not a defeat but a calculated move — his parting words are a coded message, not resignation. He trusts the institution's inherent loyalty to outlast political manipulation.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film preserves these motivations accurately. His defense of Hagrid ('I want it understood, Cornelius, that Hagrid has my full confidence'), his calm acceptance of suspension paired with the deliberate 'help will always be given' message, and his post-resolution handling of Ginny and confrontation of Malfoy all align with the book's motivational portrait.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film does not develop Dumbledore's background knowledge of Riddle as thoroughly. In the books, he says 'Brilliant... of course, he was probably the most brilliant student Hogwarts has ever seen' with an implication of long personal acquaintance and watchfulness. The film gives Dumbledore an explicit 'I taught him myself fifty years ago' line, which compensates. The film does not substantially alter or simplify his motivations — they remain protection-oriented, institutionally anchored, and strategically patient.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are intact and correctly rendered. Minor compression of the Riddle backstory context, but this is offset by the film's explicit 'I taught him myself' line. No meaningful penalty warranted.

character_arc.book_baseline: Dumbledore's arc in CoS is intentionally flat by design. He begins as the school's anchor, is temporarily removed by political machination, and returns to restore order. His departure is not a defeat — it is a tactical withdrawal with a planted message. His return confirms his institutional and moral centrality. There is no internal growth or transformation because Dumbledore is not positioned as a character undergoing change in CoS; he is a fixed point that the plot moves around.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film exactly replicates this flat arc: departure under pressure, coded parting message, return after Ginny is taken, resolution and reward. The structural beats are all present.
character_arc.difference: No meaningful difference. The arc is flat in both versions and for the same reason.
character_arc.penalty_logic: Full marks applicable per the flat-arc rule: a character can score full points if their arc is flat in the books and flat in the films.

key_relationships.book_baseline: The most important relationships in CoS are: (1) Dumbledore–Harry: mentor-protector dynamic, asymmetric trust, Dumbledore knows more than he reveals, Harry feels simultaneously supported and examined; (2) Dumbledore–Hagrid: loyal protector of someone others dismiss, Dumbledore's belief in Hagrid's innocence stretches back decades; (3) Dumbledore–Malfoy/Fudge: power contest between institutional integrity and political manipulation, Dumbledore always slightly ahead. Secondary: Dumbledore–McGonagall, functional professional partnership.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry relationship is mostly intact — the 'searching look,' the private conversation, the coded trust. The Hagrid loyalty is preserved ('I want it understood, Cornelius, that Hagrid has my full confidence'). The Malfoy dynamic is preserved in outline. The McGonagall dynamic is present in functional terms.
key_relationships.difference: The most notable compression is in the Dumbledore–Harry relationship. In the books, the post-Chamber conversation is longer and more emotionally layered: Dumbledore actively thanks Harry for loyalty ('Nothing but that could have called Fawkes to you'), then draws Harry out on the Riddle/Slytherin anxiety with patience and philosophical weight. The film retains these beats but compresses them, slightly reducing the intimacy of the exchange. Also, the book version of Dumbledore asking whether Harry has 'anything to tell him' — to which Harry withholds information — establishes a nuanced gap in the relationship (Harry doesn't fully trust even Dumbledore with everything) that is present in both versions but rendered more briefly in the film.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Relationships are mostly faithful with some compression. The Dumbledore–Harry dynamic retains its essential quality but loses some of the intimate philosophical texture. Minor deduction.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: Dumbledore's complexity in CoS comes from several sources: his oblique communication style (never saying more than necessary, letting silences carry weight); his strategic patience (not challenging Harry's lie about the car, watching rather than confronting); his combination of warmth and unsettling perception ('his twinkling light-blue gaze made Harry feel as though he were being X-rayed'); his awareness of Riddle that he holds back ('Dumbledore never seemed to like me as much as the other teachers did,' Riddle says — and Dumbledore confirms he kept a close watch); his parting message that is simultaneously a comfort and a piece of operational intelligence; and his intellectual demolition of Malfoy, which is layered and specific rather than blunt.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves the X-ray quality, the dry humor, the warm authority, and the coded parting message. The 'I taught him myself' line adds an explicit dimension to his Riddle knowledge. The Malfoy confrontation retains the chill and implication if not the full verbal architecture.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: Lost: the car-lie scene (Dumbledore's strategic silence, his choice not to press Harry on the lie — a key piece of his character's oblique patience). Lost: the more extended Malfoy rhetorical trap (the step-by-step imagined consequence for the Weasley family, the explicit identification of the political damage the diary could have done). These are both scenes that reveal Dumbledore's intelligence operating at full stretch — one through omission, one through precise articulation. Their removal simplifies him slightly without fundamentally misrepresenting him.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: The losses are real but not devastating. The car-lie omission removes an instance of strategic patience; the Malfoy compression removes an instance of intellectual precision. Neither individually nor together do they change the audience's fundamental understanding of who Dumbledore is. The complexity remains recognizable if slightly thinner. Minor deduction.

lost_or_transferred_material: Dumbledore's deliberate silence regarding Harry's lie about the flying car (book scene 17) — removes a key expression of his oblique, non-confrontational intelligence
The 'not who but how' line when examining Mrs. Norris (book scene 91) — replaced with a more direct declaration about danger, losing a characteristic piece of elliptical reasoning
The extended Malfoy confrontation in which Dumbledore walks through the political consequences of the diary use step by step (book scenes 266–270) — compressed to a chill warning in the film
The more probing 'is there anything you'd like to tell me' exchange in Dumbledore's office before Hagrid bursts in (book scene 121) — present in film but shorter and less psychologically weighted

Riddle's retrospective observation that 'Dumbledore never seemed to like me as much as the other teachers did' / 'he kept an annoyingly close watch on me' (book scenes 183–185) — not present in film corpus as Dumbledore's own demonstrable behaviour
score_caps_applied: No caps applied. Losses are real but represent minor compressions rather than transfers of agency, fundamental personality changes, or removal of defining characterization.
key_observations: The film's Dumbledore is substantially faithful to the books. His core personality — calm authority, dry wit, warm restraint, penetrating perception, and philosophical weight — is preserved across all major scenes. His structural role as institutional anchor, moral arbiter, and indirect protector is intact. His flat arc and consistent motivations are accurately rendered. The primary losses are two scenes of Dumbledore's intelligence operating in its most characteristic register: the strategic silence over Harry's lie, and the step-by-step rhetorical demolition of Malfoy. These omissions slightly thin the portrait without misrepresenting it. The film also carries over his signature physical details (half-moon spectacles, silver beard, twinkling eyes) and verbal habits (gentle irony, philosophical maxims, understated humor). The result is a Dumbledore who is recognizably and largely accurately rendered, with a score penalty reflecting real but contained compression of his most intellectually textured moments.
